newsitem.title: PERU: Peru moves to quash reports of rebel executions.
newsitem.headline: Peru moves to quash reports of rebel executions.

text.p: Peru's government moved firmly on Friday to quash reports that troops captured and then executed Marxist rebels during a spectacular military strike on the Japanese ambassador's home to free 72 hostages.

The reports have tarnished the worldwide acclaim that met the raid that freed 71 hostages and left President Alberto Fujimori's government open to charges of commiting a serious atrocity on Japanese sovereign soil.
"That is completely false. There were no executions," Fujimori told Reuters in his first interview since Tuesday's daring military strike to end the 126-day hostage crisis.

Asked if the troops had an order to kill and take no prisoners, Fujimori replied: "The order and the objective was to free the 72 hostages, not one less. We achieved freeing 72 with one who died afterwards."

Reports from military, intelligence and hostage sources had said that two of the 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels slain in the raid were shot after being captured, and that at least one more was shot while trying to surrender.
All 14 of the MRTA hostage-takers died in the raid, as did two army commandos and one of the hostages, a Peruvian judge.
An army commando who took part in the operation had said "the order was to leave no one alive. For us, the instruction was to leave no prisoners."
But the only person who had been publicly quoted as saying he knew of an execution insisted on Friday he had been misquoted.

"I have not said that at any time and it seems absolutely absurd," former hostage Rodolfo Munante, Peru's agriculture minister, told a news conference. He had been quoted by CBS/Telenoticias television as having described seeing a rebel surrender in the room where captive judges were held.

Peru's highly respected Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, a former hostage, also praised the troops' "impeccable" performance and blamed the MRTA's impossible demands for leaving Fujimori no choice but to intervene.
"I find it unfortunate that the stubborness of the terrorists in demanding impossible goals made it necessary to resort, as a last option, to force," Tudela said.

Helping to push the focus back onto the spectacular rescue mission and off the execution charges, Peruvian television showed footage of Fujimori visiting the network of tunnels used by troops to swarm into the residence in broad daylight.
The tunnels looked extremely well-built, with masonry and sturdy wooden beams, ventilation and even carpets in some places. They had at least five outlets in the house and in the surrounding gardens.
The tunnels were built by a team of 60 men working 24 hours a day for three months, and commandos waited for more than a day inside them until receiving the order to strike.

Troops used explosives to blast out of the tunnels and into the mansion -- straight into its grand reception room, where the guerrillas had laid down their weapons and taken off their shirts to play soccer in what turned out to be a fatal security lapse.

Fujimori said five rebels died in the initial explosion, while five others including leader Nestor Cerpa died rushing up a staircase. The other four were killed fighting troops in the upper story, he said.
He said the operation was intended to last six minutes but it was complicated by a stubborn 16-minute resistance by the MRTA in the house's northern wing.
An MRTA spokesman in Europe, Isaac Velazco, accused Munante of recanting his testimony about executions due to pressure from the government.

"We affirm that at different times our comrades have been given a 'coup de grace' by the Peruvian army and the Peruvian police," said Velazco by telephone from Hamburg, Germany. "Their practice has always been to kill our militants. There are cases of comrades who have been captured and have later turned up dead."
The MRTA, widely seen as a spent force and with perhaps 200 militants left alive and out of jail, threatened to carry out reprisal attacks in response to the military raid.
